title: Working at Redwood — roles, career ladders, benefits, hiring & onboarding, and internal tools
author: Aisha Malik
body:
Overview

This document consolidates the canonical guidance for working at Redwood: our ways of working, role structures and career ladders, benefits and perks, hiring and onboarding flow, and the primary internal tools new hires and managers should know. It is maintained by People Ops with input from Eng, Product, and People Managers.

1) Working at Redwood — principles and ways of working

Intro: Redwood is developer-first and engineering-led; we expect small, cross-functional teams to operate with high ownership while prioritizing clarity and psychological safety. Key principles: mission focus, measurable outcomes, and ship-safe operational practices.

Hybrid & Remote policy (summary):
- Core expectation: asynchronous-first. Teams may adopt a formal core overlap window; recommended default overlap is 11:00–16:00 PT for globally distributed teams.
- Office presence: optional weekly office day per team for sprint planning and demos; exceptions handled by managers.
- Time off: flexible PTO (manager-approved), public holidays observed per country; parental leave described below.
- Work hours & on-call: engineering teams maintain documented on-call rotations; SRE-run runbooks must be followed for escalations.

Communication norms:
- Use Slack for real-time operational comms; Confluence for long-form and runbooks; Google Drive for collaborative drafts; PRs and code review required for infra and production changes.
- All public-facing technical specs and decisions should be recorded as ADRs in confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records.

2) Roles and career ladders

High-level ladder structure (applies across Eng, Product, Design, SRE):
- IC levels: I, II, Senior (III), Staff/Principal (IV+ depending on function).
- Managerial path: Manager, Senior Manager, Director, Senior Director, VP.
- Senior individual contributor expectations are calibrated by impact, scope, and systems leadership.

Engineering ladder summary (example):
- Eng I (E1): Learning the codebase, delivering scoped features with mentorship.
- Eng II (E2): Independent delivery, clear understanding of services and testing.
- Senior Eng (E3): Leads medium-sized initiatives, mentors peers, contributes to design reviews.
- Staff Eng (E4): Technical lead across services, defines cross-team architecture and reliability improvements.

Promotion & review cadence:
1. Performance reviews: biannual (mid-year and year-end).
2. Promotion window: candidates can be nominated any time; formal packet typically prepared ahead of the next review cycle.
3. Promotion packet components: role-specific rubric, manager assessment, peer feedback, impact examples, and proposed level.
4. Decision: promotion committee (People Ops + function leads) reviews packets and communicates decisions within 6–8 weeks.

Promotion criteria table (summary):
| Dimension | Eng II | Senior Eng | Staff Eng |
|-----------|--------|------------|----------:|
| Scope | Component | Multiple components | Cross-team / product area |
| Autonomy | Works with guidance | Independent | Sets direction and drives alignment |
| Impact | Feature delivery | Feature + reliability | Strategic product/infra impact |
| Mentorship | Learns from seniors | Mentors others | Develops leaders across teams |

3) Benefits & perks (high-level summary)

Health & wellness:
- Medical, dental, and vision plans with multiple tiers. Redwood covers a significant portion of employee premiums; coverage varies by country.
- Mental health: confidential EAP and therapy stipend.

Compensation & equity:
- Competitive base salary bands per level; annual calibration and refresh cycles.
- Equity grants: new hires receive an initial grant; refresh/refreshers tied to performance and role changes.

Leave programs:
- Parental leave: primary caretaker leave up to 20 weeks (country-dependent), secondary caregiver leave up to 8 weeks.
- Care & sick leave: flexible paid sick time and caregiver allowances.

Learning & development:
- Learning stipend: annual stipend for conferences, courses, and books.
- Internal mentorship and career development workshops run quarterly.

Work setup & allowances:
- Home office stipend (one-time) and annual ergonomic refresh budget.
- Commuter benefit where local offices are open.
- Hardware: standard laptop + optional secondary monitor; upgrade policy described in eng-developer-experience/sdk-guides.

Other perks:
- Team event budget, wellness reimbursements, hack days, and volunteer days.

4) Hiring overview (process & guidelines)

Hiring principles:
- Hire for mission alignment, technical competency, and collaborative mindset.
- Focus on candidate experience: timely communication and transparent feedback.

Typical interview stages (example for engineering roles):
1. Recruiter screen (30–45m): role fit, compensation expectations, basic logistics.
2. Technical screen (45–60m): coding or systems design depending on level.
3. On-site / loop (2–4 interviews, virtual or in-person): coding, design, behavioral, and a hiring manager conversation.
4. Offer & references: People Ops coordinates offer approval, reference checks, and background verification.

Interview guidelines for interviewers:
- Use standard scorecards (behavioral / technical) and provide written notes within 48 hours.
- Diverse interview panels encouraged; avoid panel fatigue by scheduling breaks and limiting to 4 interviews per loop.

Offer & negotiation notes:
- Compensation includes base, bonus (where applicable), and equity; offers are approved by Hiring Committee and Finance.
- Relay offers through People Ops; managers may discuss role-level expectations but must not promise unapproved exceptions.

5) Onboarding — first 90 days checklist

Pre-boarding (before day 1):
- Complete offer docs, sign policies, set up SSO, hardware shipped.
- People Ops assigns a buddy and schedules an orientation session.

Day 1–7 (orientation & access):
1. Orientation with People Ops (company overview, benefits overview, Code of Conduct).
2. Manager 1:1 to set 30/60/90 goals.
3. Access provisioning: GitHub, Jira, Confluence, CI systems, Slack, internal VPN — confirm access by Day 3.
4. Complete security training and data handling checklist.

Week 2–4 (ramp & early delivery):
- Small onboarding project assigned (bugfix or small feature) with clear acceptance criteria.
- Team hush meeting: product and roadmap overview, service ownership, and runbooks review.

Months 2–3 (scope & impact):
- Deliver onboarding project, present a 30-day learnings update, and collaborate on backlog items.
- First performance sync and development conversation with manager at 60 days.

Onboarding checklist (numbered):
1. Confirm hardware and home-office stipend processed.
2. Verify access to required repos and CI/CD pipelines.
3. Complete security & privacy training modules.
4. Meet assigned buddy and complete scheduled 1:1s.
5. Ship first onboarding commit and request a review.

6) Internal tools guide (quick reference)

Primary tools and purpose:
- Slack: real-time communication, incident channels (#incidents, #sre-oncall).
- Confluence: canonical docs, runbooks, ADRs. Use templates under confluence/architecture-and-standards.
- GitHub: source control, PRs required for prod infra changes. Branching strategy documented in eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build.
- Jira: issue tracking; create tickets with clear acceptance criteria and link to PRs.
- CI/CD (internal): builds and deploy pipelines; owners and runbooks in eng-platform/runbooks.
- VPN & SSO (Okta): single sign-on for production consoles and access controls. Follow security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth for RBAC requests.

Account & access requests:
- Request access via the Access Request form in Confluence (template) or the Slack /ops-bot. Include justification, owner, and required expiration date.
- For production access, provide a manager approval screenshot and ensure 2FA is configured.

Dev environment recommendations:
- Use the supported dev container image (repo: eng-developer-experience/dev-containers).
- Local testing: run unit tests and linting before opening a PR; CI will run integration tests.

Incident & escalation channels:
1. P0 incident: page the on-call SRE, open an incident in PagerDuty, and notify #incidents in Slack.
2. Follow the Incident Response Runbook: identify impact, mitigation steps, RCA owner, and comms plan.
3. Post-incident: create a postmortem and link to oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems.

7) Ownership and contacts

Maintained by: People Ops (primary), with contributions from Eng leaders and Security.
Document owner: Aisha Malik (People Ops).
Escalation contacts: People Ops mailbox people-ops@redwood.example.com; Security triage security@redwood.example.com; IT & hardware support it-support@redwood.example.com.

8) Change management and how to propose updates

- To propose a change to this handbook page, copy this page to your personal Confluence draft, annotate proposed edits, and request a reviewer from People Ops.
- Major policy changes (e.g., leave programs, equity, or office policy) require review by Finance, Legal, and People Ops and a town-hall announcement.

Appendix A — Quick links & templates
- New hire orientation template: /confluence/company-handbook/company-handbook-working-at-redwood-orientation-template
- Promotion packet template: /confluence/company-handbook/promotion-packet-template
- Access request form: /confluence/policies-and-process/access-and-permissions/access-request-template

Appendix B — Example 30/60/90 template
- 30 days: learn codebase, complete onboarding project, meet key cross-functional partners.
- 60 days: own a small feature or bugfix end-to-end, contribute to design discussion.
- 90 days: deliver measurable product or infra change and present outcomes.

If you have questions or suggested edits, contact the document owner or file a People Ops request via the People Ops intake form.
